scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Hi IT!! The campus network keeps going SLOW in bursts.
Something around the main router box must be overloaded, I think, but I don't
know which one or why. Could someone look at it and make the network stop
crawling!!! Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: FRR RIP routing on router2. The dynamic routing process is misconfigured, so router2 is not advertising its LANs to the rest of the campus.

Mechanism: Because router2 does not participate in RIP on any interface, router1 (the central router) never learns routes to the networks behind router2 (servers 1.0.0.0/8 and “internet lab” 128.168.0.0/16). Clients on office/CS/IT/Principal subnets send traffic toward those destinations and then stall while the stack retries and times out, which feels like periodic “slow bursts.” Local traffic within each site remains fast.

Localization: On router2, “show running” shows router rip with only “version 2” and no network statements. On router1, “show ip route” contains RIP-learned routes to router0’s 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24 via 10.10.0.1, but no routes to 1.0.0.0/8 or 128.168.0.0/16. Pings from router1 to 1.0.0.5 and 128.168.0.2 fail (rc=2). From office_pc, iperf to pc1/pc2 returns “Network is unreachable,” while local office-to-principal ping is fine.

Root cause: Missing RIP “network” statements on router2, so its routes are never advertised to router1/router0.

Corrective fix: Configure router2’s RIP to advertise its interfaces:
- router rip
  version 2
  network 20.0.0.0/8   (r1–r2 link)
  network 1.0.0.0/8    (servers LAN)
  network 128.168.0.0/16 (internet lab LAN)
write memory
Then verify on router1: “show ip route” includes R routes to 1.0.0.0/8 and 128.168.0.0/16 and end-to-end pings succeed. As a follow-up, consider replacing public/very large masks with RFC1918 subnets and /30-/31 P2P links to avoid ARP/broadcast bloat.

per_axis.rationale: The submission never notes router0's baseline health (ip_forward enabled, interfaces up, and 0% transit loss) and instead diagnoses router2 RIP misconfiguration.

The investigation log shows router2's FRR config lacks RIP network statements and multiple reachability tests (pings, ip route gets, iperf) to addresses behind router2 fail, supporting the agent's conclusion; a few specific assertions (e.g. exact next-hop via 10.10.0.1, some named subnets) are not directly shown in the log, so grounding is not perfect. Overall the inference that missing RIP advertisement on router2 explains the observed unreachable destinations follows logically and the essential checks were performed.
